clue.text: Ran away with the Spanish [This needs work – ed.]

blocks.note: el is the Spanish word for 'the'
OP, short for opus, is a musical work
the abbreviation for editor, used as letters

explanation.surface: A setter has handed in an unfinished clue, and the crossword editor has scribbled a complaint in square brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: The editor's bracketed note looks like an aside about the puzzle, but it carries the second half of the wordplay: the clue really does 'need work' and an editor.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is to run off secretly, usually with a lover, to marry without permission.

clue.text: Departed After the scheduled time

blocks.note: first meaning: dead, as when we speak of 'the departed'
second meaning: not on time, overdue

explanation.walkthrough: 'Departed' reads like a train leaving, which chimes with the timetable sense; in fact it means deceased, the other meaning of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a polite adjective for someone recently deceased and also the everyday adjective for arriving behind schedule.

clue.text: Rogue openly wrapping article in packaging material

indicators.note: a rogue goes astray and behaves unpredictably, so these letters leave their usual order
to wrap something is to go all round it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: the six letters of this word rearranged
the definite article

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is caught brazenly gift-wrapping some item in packaging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rogue' looks like the subject of the sentence, a villain, but it is the signal to rearrange the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Polythene is the common plastic used for bags, film and wrapping goods for transport and sale.

clue.text: Scottish king is able to follow horse

blocks.note: a dun is a greyish-brown horse
'can' means is able

explanation.surface: A Scottish monarch proves capable of riding behind a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'follow' puts the second piece below the first, so the horse comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Duncan was an eleventh-century ruler of Scotland, famous as the monarch murdered in Shakespeare's Macbeth.

clue.text: Comes into home with heartless, reclusive people

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

blocks.note: 'in' means at home
hermits, with the middle letter M removed

explanation.surface: Someone walks into the house accompanied by unfeeling hermits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes into' reads as entering a room, but it is the phrase for receiving a legacy.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into money or property is the idiom for receiving it as an heir after someone dies.

clue.text: Tailor Swift led by prince and idiots

indicators.note: to tailor is to cut and refashion, so the letters are remade into a new order

blocks.note: Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare's history plays
the five letters of the singer's surname rearranged

explanation.surface: Taylor Swift, punningly spelt, follows a royal into the company of fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor Swift' is a pun on the pop star Taylor Swift, so 'Tailor' looks like part of a name; it is the anagram signal. 'Led by' puts the prince in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are colloquial insults for foolish or stupid people, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Tory Blair finally is given greeting

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the very end of the word, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: last letter of the former Labour leader's name
taken as written
a casual hello

explanation.surface: A Conservative greets Tony Blair at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory Blair' looks like a jibe at Tony Blair, but 'Tory' is the definition and Blair only supplies one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rishi Sunak led the Conservative Party and was prime minister, so his first name stands for one Tory politician.

clue.text: Trends of new boring scene [Fixed with edit]

indicators.note: a drill bores into something, so one piece goes inside the other
a thing that is fixed has been repaired and put back together differently

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter's broken clue about trends in some scene, with the editor noting it has now been mended.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an editorial aside, yet 'Fixed' is the anagram signal and 'edit' is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tendencies are general drifts or inclinations in behaviour, which is what trends are.

clue.text: Mythical hunter from America, in American capital

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
the state capital of Georgia, USA

explanation.surface: A legendary huntress turns out to come from the USA, specifically from one of its capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American capital' suggests Washington, but any US state capital will do; Atlanta is Georgia's.
explanation.definitionFit: Atalanta was the swift-footed huntress of Greek legend, famous for the Calydonian boar hunt and her footrace.

clue.text: Latin song? [Needs rewriting, along with 1 Down]

indicators.note: rewriting means setting the material down again in a new form

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A clue about a Latin song, with the editor grumbling that it and a 1 Down clue must be redone.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no 1 Down in the grid, which makes the bracket look like a genuine editorial note; '1' gives a letter and 'Down' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A team that is down is behind in the score, which means it is currently trailing in the game.

clue.text: French composer and wife getting into more hackneyed, factual author

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so one piece ends up within the other

blocks.note: Maurice Ravel, composer of Boléro
standard abbreviation
trite means hackneyed; this is its comparative

explanation.surface: A French composer and his spouse turn their hand to stale non-fiction writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The composer and wife are joined first, then together placed inside the comparative of trite.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who writes about journeys and places produces non-fiction, so this writer is one kind of factual author.

clue.text: At intervals, action seems a viable plan for film buff

indicators.note: things at intervals are spaced out, so only every other letter is used

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters
taken as written
in British slang a goer is an idea or scheme that will work

explanation.surface: Periodic bursts of action make a film fan think a plan could work.
explanation.walkthrough: A goer is British slang for a proposal that is likely to succeed: 'the plan is a goer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who regularly goes to the pictures is a keen fan of films, so a film buff.

clue.text: Barrack and Michelle ultimately getting huge backing

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is kept
going backwards means the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: a synonym of huge
last letter of the name

explanation.surface: The Obamas receive enormous support, the misspelt first name pointing at Barack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrack' looks like a misspelling of Barack Obama, but with two Rs it is the British verb meaning to jeer or heckle.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack is to heckle or shout insults at someone, and to gibe is to jeer or taunt them.

clue.text: Bird, one repeatedly around Lake

blocks.note: a small songbird
the Roman numeral
CA, short for circa (around), given twice

explanation.surface: A bird, a lone one, keeps circling a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' reads as a direction to place one piece round another, but here it is simply the Latin abbreviation ca., doubled by 'repeatedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Titicaca is the large freshwater lake on the border between Peru and Bolivia, high in the Andes.

clue.text: Scottish mountain accountant’s climbing on amazing mornirg

indicators.note: something amazing leaves you confused, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: CA is a chartered accountant; the 's is 'is'
the seven letters of this misspelt word rearranged

explanation.surface: An accountant scales a Scottish peak on a glorious morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mornirg' looks like a typo for morning, but it is exactly the letters needed. In a down clue, 'on' puts the accountant above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairn Gorm is a peak in the Cairngorms range of the Scottish Highlands, home to a ski resort.

clue.text: Oddly bluesy cover of Satchmo giving good wish

indicators.note: behaving oddly is behaving strangely, so the letters fall out of their normal order
a cover sits on the outside, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of Louis Armstrong's nickname

explanation.surface: An eccentric bluesy cover version of a Louis Armstrong number serves as a kindly sentiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' wants to mean taking odd letters, but those don't fit; it signals an anagram. 'Cover' is a musical cover version on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a benediction, a wish for someone's welfare, spoken especially after a sneeze.

clue.text: Safe king avoids appearance in massacre

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep away from it, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: criminal slang for a safe; a safebreaker is a peterman
look, with the K for king removed
K is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch keeps out of sight to stay safe during a slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like an adjective (out of danger), but it is the noun, in old thieves' slang a peter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peterloo Massacre of 1819 saw cavalry charge a reform rally in Manchester, killing protesters.

clue.text: Expression of understanding [A bit imprecise – ed.]

indicators.note: a bit is only a part, so the answer is a small piece of the following letters

blocks.note: found across the end of one word and the next, ignoring the dash

explanation.surface: An editor flags a clue as slightly vague.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as an editor's complaint that the clue is woolly, but its letters run on into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying this phrase tells a speaker that you have followed and grasped what they mean.

clue.text: Where we get crude lass turning up after cry for attention

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: a shout of 'oi!' to get someone's attention
a synonym

explanation.surface: Someone shouts for attention and a vulgar young woman shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crude' looks like vulgar describing the lass, but it is crude oil, so the definition is a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude oil is extracted from beneath the sea by drilling platforms, so they are where it comes from.

clue.text: Energy emission stopped by east German broadcaster

indicators.note: a gap stopped up is filled, so something is plugged into the middle

blocks.note: energy given off as waves or particles
Ost is the German word for east

explanation.surface: Radioactive leakage halted by an East German broadcaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'east German' suggests the old East Germany, but it means the German word for east.
explanation.definitionFit: A station that transmits programmes over the airwaves is an organisation that broadcasts.

clue.text: I love mostly pleasant; architectural style

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
nice, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone declares an architectural style mostly agreeable to them.
explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon splits wordplay from definition; 'I love' looks like a statement but gives two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionic is one of the classical orders of Greek building, recognised by the scroll-shaped capitals on its columns.

clue.text: Navy party clothes for a Bond villain

indicators.note: as a verb, to clothe is to dress or cover, so one piece is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: a do is a party
the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Navy-blue party outfits worn by a 007 baddie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Navy' looks like a colour and 'clothes' like garments; they are the Royal Navy and a verb meaning dresses.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr No is the title villain of the first James Bond film, released in 1962.

clue.text: Conservative, gutless Tory, hosts Posh and Berks?

indicators.note: with the guts gone only the shell remains, so just the outside letters stay
a host takes in guests, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
first and last letters
U means upper-class, as in 'U and non-U'

explanation.surface: A spineless Conservative entertains the Beckhams, Posh Spice and the Berkshire set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' suggests Victoria Beckham, and 'Berks' is British slang for idiots; Berks is in fact Berkshire, an English county, and the question mark flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Berkshire is one of the English shires, so it is an instance of the administrative region, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Pig covered in fat left for sailors

indicators.note: to be covered in something is to be coated all over, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a male pig
pig fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: A pig smeared in lard is abandoned to the ship's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as abandoned, but it is the direction; the definition is a sailor's word for that side.
explanation.definitionFit: Larboard is the old nautical term for the port side of a ship, on your left facing forward.

clue.text: Rule out / what spin doctors do [Faulty clue – ed.]

indicators.note: something faulty is broken, so its letters are reassembled in another order

blocks.note: public relations, the spin doctor's trade
the six letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A clue split by a slash between definition and wordplay, which the editor has marked as broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like the editor rejecting the clue, but 'Faulty' is the anagram signal and 'clue' and 'ed.' are its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To preclude something is to prevent it or make it impossible, which is to exclude it.

clue.text: Prance Harry blog probed by American

indicators.note: to harry is to harass and disturb, so the letters are knocked out of place
a probe goes into something, so one piece is pushed inside the other

blocks.note: the four letters of this word rearranged
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Prince Harry's online diary is investigated by an American, perhaps his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prance Harry' plays on Prince Harry, so Harry looks like a name; it is a verb signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To gambol is to skip or leap about playfully, much as a lamb frisks, so it means to caper.
